content: Carolina horsenettle, scientifically known as Solanum carolinense, is also referred to by various other names, including Bull nettle, Horse nettle, Apple of Sodom, Radical Weed, Sand Brier, and Tread-softly. Despite its name, it is not a true nettle but belongs to the Solanaceae family, commonly known as the nightshade family. This plant is characterized by its painful spines, which grow along the stems, penetrate the skin upon contact, and often break off, causing irritation. Carolina horsenettle is a perennial, herbaceous plant that is native to the southeastern United States but has spread extensively across North America. The leaves of this plant are arranged alternately along the stem and are elliptic-oblong to oval in shape. They are irregularly lobed or coarsely toothed, with both surfaces covered in fine hairs. The flowers of the plant typically have five petals and are either white or purple with yellow centers, although a blue variant exists that resembles the flowers of tomato plants. The fruits of the Carolina horsenettle also bear a resemblance to tomatoes. When immature, the fruits are dark green with light green stripes, but as they mature, they turn yellow and develop a wrinkled texture. Each fruit contains approximately 60 seeds. The plant flowers throughout the summer, from April to October. All parts of the Carolina horsenettle are toxic. The green, unripe fruits are particularly dangerous and have been known to poison both children and cattle when ingested. The mature fruits are believed to be either non-toxic or significantly less toxic. This plant is commonly found in pastures, along roadsides, near railroad tracks, and in disturbed or waste areas. It typically grows to a height of about 1 meter but is often shorter, existing as a subshrub. It thrives in sandy or loamy soils. Carolina horsenettle is classified as a noxious weed in several U.S. states. It has the ability to spread both vegetatively through underground rhizomes and by seed. The plant is resistant to many herbicides, and in some cases, the use of herbicides can inadvertently promote its growth by eliminating competing weeds. Gardeners who attempt to remove the plant manually often find it particularly troublesome due to its spines, which can penetrate the skin and break off, as well as its deep root system, which makes it difficult to eradicate. The plant is sometimes written as horse nettle or horse-nettle, although the USDA typically uses the spelling horsenettle. Additional common names for the plant include Wild tomato, Devil's tomato, and Sand Briar.
